e: The n+1 rule is a simplification that works cleanly only when all relevant coupling constants are similar; unequal coupling constants to different sets of neighbors produce more complex patterns that must be analyzed as separate couplings rather than a single n+1 multiplet.

q: Rank the following methyl groups from most upfield to most downfield based on typical ¹H NMR chemical shift: CH3 attached to a plain alkyl carbon, CH3 attached
e: Plain alkyl CH3 is least deshielded (around 0.9 ppm); a carbonyl-adjacent CH3 is pulled somewhat downfield (around 2.1 ppm) by the electron-withdrawing carbonyl; an aromatic-ring CH3 is shifted further by ring anisotropy (around 2.3 ppm); and an O-CH3 is most deshielded (around 3.3-3.8 ppm) by the directly attached electronegative oxygen.

q: Why do long-range couplings across four or more bonds usually fail to produce visible splitting in a routine ¹H NMR spectrum of a simple flexible molecule?
e: Coupling is transmitted through bonding electrons, and its magnitude typically shrinks quickly as the number of intervening bonds grows, so beyond three bonds the coupling constant in a flexible, saturated system is usually too small to resolve as visible splitting.

q: An ethanol sample's O-H proton integrates to 1H in theory, but the measured integration can vary noticeably between samples and conditions. The most likely expl
e: Because O-H protons exchange rapidly with any available exchangeable protons (like trace water), the effective population and position of this signal is sensitive to moisture and sample purity, making its integration and shift less reproducible than for non-exchangeable C-H protons.

q: Given that aromatic ring protons are deshielded by the ring's induced magnetic field while a proton located directly above or below the ring plane (if one exist
e: Anisotropic shielding effects, like those from aromatic rings, alkenes, and alkynes, depend on where a proton sits relative to the induced field lines, which is why the same functional group can deshield some nearby protons while shielding others in a different spatial position.

q: Two protons related by an internal mirror plane of symmetry within an otherwise achiral, conformationally averaged molecule will typically give the same ¹H NMR
e: Protons related by a genuine symmetry operation of the molecule, such as reflection through an internal mirror plane, occupy equivalent environments on a time-averaged basis and therefore resonate at the same chemical shift.

q: ¹³C NMR typically shows each chemically distinct carbon as:
e: ¹³C is only ~1.1% natural abundance, so two ¹³C atoms are rarely adjacent — carbon-carbon coupling is negligible, giving simple, usually unsplit peaks (with standard decoupling).

q: A carbonyl carbon in ¹³C NMR typically appears:
e: Carbonyl carbons are strongly deshielded by the adjacent electronegative, pi-bonded oxygen, pushing their signal far downfield (160–220 ppm).

q: Why is ¹³C NMR generally less sensitive (requiring more sample/scans) than ¹H NMR?
e: Both the rarity of the ¹³C isotope and its inherently weaker NMR signal (lower gyromagnetic ratio) compared to ¹H make ¹³C NMR much less sensitive, requiring longer acquisition times.

q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, each peak generally corresponds to:
e: Each unique carbon environment gives rise to its own peak, regardless of how many hydrogens are attached to that carbon, which is different from how ¹H NMR integration works.

q: A ketone or aldehyde carbonyl carbon in ¹³C NMR typically appears in roughly what chemical shift range, making it the most downfield common signal?
e: Carbonyl carbons are strongly deshielded by the attached oxygen and the carbon's bonding, placing their signals well downfield of essentially all other common carbon environments.

q: ¹³C NMR spectra are referenced to tetramethylsilane (TMS), just as ¹H NMR spectra are, with TMS's carbons defined as 0 ppm.
e: TMS is used as the zero-point reference for both ¹H and ¹³C NMR because its carbons (and protons) are highly shielded, inert, and give a single clean reference peak.

q: The typical chemical shift range for ¹³C NMR signals (roughly 0-220 ppm) is much wider than for ¹H NMR (roughly 0-12 ppm). This is best explained by:
e: Because carbon sits at the center of bonding with more direct exposure to hybridization and substituent effects, its chemical shift is more sensitive to structural differences, spreading ¹³C signals over a much wider ppm range than ¹H signals.

q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, peak height or area reliably indicates the number of carbons contributing to that signal, the same way integrat
e: Differences in relaxation times and the nuclear Overhauser effect between different carbons (especially quaternary versus protonated carbons) make simple peak height or area an unreliable guide to the number of carbons in ¹³C NMR, unlike in ¹H NMR.

q: Aromatic ring carbons typically appear in ¹³C NMR in roughly what chemical shift region?
e: The delocalized pi system and partial double-bond character of aromatic carbons deshield them into the roughly 100-150 ppm region, distinct from both simple alkyl carbons and carbonyl carbons.

q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, why do we typically NOT observe splitting of one carbon's signal due to coupling with a neighboring carbon (car
e: Because ¹³C is rare (about 1.1 percent natural abundance), the odds that two bonded carbons are both the ¹³C isotope in the same molecule are very low, so carbon-carbon coupling is statistically almost never observed in a routine spectrum.

q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, each carbon peak typically appears as a single, unsplit line even though most carbons have one or more attached
e: A decoupling pulse sequence continuously flips the attached protons' spins during the ¹³C experiment, averaging out C-H coupling so each unique carbon gives one clean singlet instead of a complex multiplet.

q: A ketone's carbonyl carbon (around 205-220 ppm) appears at a higher chemical shift than an ester's carbonyl carbon (around 165-175 ppm). This difference is main
e: The ester oxygen's lone pair donates into the carbonyl pi system by resonance, increasing electron density at the carbonyl carbon and shielding it relative to a ketone, which lacks that extra donating oxygen.

q: Alkyne carbons typically appear around 65-90 ppm in ¹³C NMR, noticeably more upfield than alkene or aromatic carbons (roughly 100-150 ppm), even though all are
e: The linear, cylindrically symmetric pi system of a triple bond interacts with the applied field differently than a planar double bond's pi system, producing an anisotropic effect that shields sp alkyne carbons relative to sp2 alkene or aromatic carbons.

q: Because of its molecular symmetry, how many distinct ¹³C NMR signals would toluene (methylbenzene) show, given that the ring carbons pair up by symmetry?
e: Toluene has a mirror plane that makes the two carbons ortho to the methyl group equivalent to each other, and the two meta carbons equivalent to each other, giving five unique carbons total: the methyl carbon, the ipso carbon, the equivalent ortho pair, the equivalent meta pair, and the para carbon.

q: In a DEPT experiment, quaternary carbons (carbons with no attached hydrogens) are distinguished from CH, CH2, and CH3 carbons because:
e: DEPT transfers polarization from attached protons to the carbon nucleus, so a carbon with no attached hydrogens has nothing to receive that transfer from and simply does not show up in the DEPT spectrum.

q: Quaternary carbons typically show weaker peak intensities in a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum compared to protonated carbons of similar abundance.
e: Quaternary carbons lack the nuclear Overhauser enhancement from directly attached protons and often relax more slowly, both of which tend to make their signals weaker relative to protonated carbons, even at equal molar amounts.

q: Between a simple aldehyde's carbonyl carbon and a simple ketone's carbonyl carbon, which is generally found further downfield in ¹³C NMR?
e: Ketone carbonyl carbons typically fall around 205-220 ppm, while aldehyde carbonyl carbons are usually a bit more shielded, around 190-205 ppm, due to differences in the groups attached to the carbonyl carbon.

q: An sp3 carbon directly attached to a hydroxyl oxygen (as in an alcohol) typically appears around 50-90 ppm in ¹³C NMR, well downfield of a typical alkane carbon
e: Oxygen's electronegativity pulls electron density away from the carbon it is bonded to, deshielding that carbon and shifting its signal downfield relative to an ordinary alkane carbon.

q: Two carbons related by an internal mirror plane of symmetry in an achiral molecule will typically give the same ¹³C NMR chemical shift.
e: Just as with ¹H NMR, carbons related by a genuine symmetry operation of the molecule occupy chemically equivalent environments and therefore resonate at the same shift.

q: A carboxylic acid's carbonyl carbon (roughly 170-185 ppm) and an ester's carbonyl carbon (roughly 165-175 ppm) can sometimes be distinguished mainly by:
e: The shift ranges for these two carbonyl types overlap somewhat, so chemists often combine the ¹³C shift with other evidence, such as the presence of a broad O-H absorption in IR or an O-H proton in ¹H NMR, to tell them apart confidently.

q: A nitrile carbon (C of a C≡N group) typically appears around 115-120 ppm in ¹³C NMR, a range that is useful diagnostically mainly because:
e: Although close to the aromatic/alkene region, a nitrile carbon's shift around 115-120 ppm, especially combined with a sharp triple-bond stretch in IR, helps distinguish it from other unsaturated carbons.

q: A para-disubstituted benzene ring with two different substituents, which breaks the ring's six-fold symmetry down to a single mirror plane, would be expected to
e: The mirror plane running through the two substituted carbons makes the two carbons next to one substituent equivalent to each other, and the two carbons next to the other substituent equivalent to each other, giving four unique aromatic carbons: the two substituted carbons plus the two equivalent pairs.

q: Why do we not typically observe carbon-carbon (¹³C-¹³C) spin coupling in a routine ¹³C NMR spectrum, even though carbons are directly bonded to each other throu
e: Since roughly 99 percent of carbon atoms are the spin-inactive ¹²C isotope, the probability that a given ¹³C nucleus happens to be bonded to another ¹³C nucleus is small, so carbon-carbon coupling is rarely visible above the noise in a normal spectrum.

q: A molecule can sometimes show a different total number of distinct ¹H NMR signals than distinct ¹³C NMR signals for the same structure. What is one reasonable e
e: Because chemical shift differences and coincidental overlaps differ between ¹H and ¹³C environments, and because symmetry can relate protons without necessarily relating the carbons carrying them (or vice versa), the number of resolved signals does not have to match between the two spectra.

q: In a DEPT-135 experiment, CH and CH3 carbons appear as positive peaks, CH2 carbons appear as negative (inverted) peaks, and quaternary carbons are absent altoge
e: Because DEPT signal phase and intensity depend on the number of attached protons, comparing a DEPT-135 spectrum to the standard ¹³C spectrum lets chemists sort carbons into CH3/CH, CH2, and quaternary categories, something ordinary ¹³C peak height cannot reliably do.

q: ¹³C NMR chemical shifts generally follow the same electronegativity-based deshielding trends seen in ¹H NMR, where attaching a more electronegative atom shifts
e: Both techniques respond to the same underlying electron-withdrawing inductive and resonance effects, so electronegative substituents deshield nearby carbons in ¹³C NMR in a way that parallels ¹H NMR trends, even though the absolute ppm shifts differ in scale.

q: Neopentane, (CH3)4C, has five carbon atoms but shows only two signals in ¹³C NMR. This is best explained by:
e: The four methyl groups are related by the molecule's high symmetry (effectively a tetrahedral arrangement around the central carbon), making them all chemically equivalent and giving just one methyl signal plus one signal for the unique central quaternary carbon.

q: Obtaining a good ¹³C NMR spectrum often requires longer acquisition times or more scans rather than simply increasing sample concentration, partly because:
e: Slow relaxation, particularly for quaternary carbons lacking nearby protons to help them relax, limits how quickly a ¹³C signal can be repeatedly sampled, so extending the number of scans (not just raising concentration) is often needed to achieve a usable spectrum.

q: Rank the following carbonyl-containing carbons from LOWEST to HIGHEST typical ¹³C chemical shift: amide carbonyl, ester carbonyl, ketone carbonyl.
e: The amide nitrogen donates electron density into the carbonyl most effectively by resonance, shielding its carbon the most, followed by the ester oxygen's somewhat weaker donation, while the ketone, lacking this extra heteroatom donation, appears furthest downfield.

q: In ¹³C NMR, a carbon's chemical shift is strongly affected by nearby electronegative atoms even two or three bonds away, similar to the pattern seen in ¹H NMR,
e: Inductive electron withdrawal from an electronegative atom propagates through several bonds in both ¹H and ¹³C NMR, deshielding nearby nuclei, with the effect weakening as the number of intervening bonds increases.

q: In mass spectrometry, the molecular ion peak (M+) corresponds to:
e: The molecular ion forms when the neutral molecule loses an electron in the ionization source, giving a radical cation at the molecule’s full mass.

q: A mass spec fragmentation pattern showing loss of 15 mass units from the molecular ion is most consistent with loss of:
e: A mass loss of 15 corresponds to CH₃ (methyl, 12+3=15), a very common fragmentation for molecules with a methyl group attached to a stabilizing center.

q: In mass spectrometry, the "base peak" refers to:
e: The base peak is defined as the most intense peak in the spectrum (100% relative abundance) — it is often, but not always, the same as the molecular ion peak.

q: In mass spectrometry, the term m/z refers to:
e: Mass spectrometers separate and detect ions based on their mass-to-charge ratio, m/z, which for most singly charged ions in an intro course is essentially equal to the ion's mass.

q: In electron ionization (EI) mass spectrometry, the molecular ion is typically formed by:
e: A high-energy electron beam knocks one electron out of the neutral molecule, leaving behind an odd-electron, positively charged species called the molecular ion or radical cation.

q: The molecular ion peak (M+) always corresponds to the most intense peak in the entire mass spectrum.
e: The most intense peak is called the base peak, and it is very often a fragment ion rather than the molecular ion, especially for molecules that fragment easily; M+ itself can be weak or even absent for some compounds.

q: The relative height of the M+1 isotope peak compared to M+ in a mass spectrum is mainly useful for estimating:
e: Since about 1.1 percent of carbon atoms are naturally ¹³C, the M+1 peak's relative intensity grows roughly in proportion to the number of carbons present, giving a rough estimate of carbon count.

q: A compound containing a single chlorine atom typically shows an M+2 peak with what approximate relative intensity compared to M+?
e: Chlorine's two natural isotopes, 35Cl and 37Cl, occur in roughly a 3:1 ratio, so a single-chlorine compound's M+2 peak (containing 37Cl) appears at roughly one-third the height of the M+ peak (containing 35Cl).

q: A compound containing a single bromine atom typically shows M+ and M+2 peaks of roughly what relative intensity to each other?
e: Bromine's two natural isotopes, 79Br and 81Br, occur in nearly equal abundance, so a single-bromine compound shows M+ and M+2 peaks of roughly similar height, a distinctive pattern compared to chlorine.

q: Loss of a methyl radical, corresponding to a mass loss of 15 units, from the molecular ion is a common fragmentation for branched alkyl compounds.
e: Cleaving off a methyl group is a frequent and often favorable fragmentation pathway, especially when it generates a more stable remaining cation, which is common in branched structures.

q: A mass spectral fragment showing a loss of 18 mass units from the molecular ion most commonly indicates loss of:
e: Loss of 18 mass units corresponds to H2O, a very common fragmentation pathway for alcohols (and some other oxygen-containing compounds) under electron ionization conditions.

q: The nitrogen rule states that, for typical organic compounds containing only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and similar common elements, the molecular weig
e: Because nitrogen has an odd valence (typically three bonds) while carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen follow patterns that keep the overall mass even in their absence, each nitrogen atom added in a stable structure shifts the molecular weight's parity, making an odd number of nitrogens correspond to an odd molecular weight.

q: A loss of 28 mass units from a molecular ion is ambiguous on its own because it could correspond to either:
e: Both CO (common from ketones, aldehydes, and aromatic ethers) and C2H4 (common from retro-type eliminations) have a mass of 28, so this loss alone does not uniquely identify the fragmentation pathway without additional supporting evidence.

q: Alpha cleavage, the preferential breaking of a bond adjacent to a heteroatom such as nitrogen or oxygen, is a favorable fragmentation pathway mainly because:
e: When the bond next to an oxygen or nitrogen breaks, the heteroatom's lone pair can donate into the resulting cation through resonance, stabilizing it and making that fragmentation pathway especially favorable.

q: A McLafferty rearrangement in a carbonyl-containing compound requires the presence of what structural feature, and produces what kind of products?
e: The McLafferty rearrangement requires a gamma-hydrogen relative to the carbonyl so that a six-membered transition state can form, transferring that hydrogen and cleaving a bond to release a neutral alkene while leaving behind a stable, even-electron cation.

q: The characteristic tropylium cation at m/z 91 is commonly observed in the mass spectra of which class of compounds?
e: Benzylic cleavage of an alkylbenzene's side chain generates a benzylic cation that readily rearranges into the highly stable, resonance-delocalized seven-membered tropylium cation, observed at m/z 91.

q: More highly branched alkanes generally show a weaker molecular ion peak than their straight-chain isomers, because branching provides additional, more easily ac
e: Branch points allow formation of more stable secondary or tertiary carbocations upon fragmentation, making it energetically easier for the branched molecular ion to fall apart rather than survive intact, weakening the M+ peak relative to a straight-chain isomer.

q: A loss of 43 mass units from a molecular ion commonly corresponds to loss of which fragment(s)?
e: Both the isopropyl radical (C3H7, mass 43) and the acetyl cation-forming group (CH3CO, also mass 43) are common fragments lost from molecular ions, so a loss of 43 alone is often ambiguous without further context.

q: In the mass spectrum of a simple aldehyde, a loss of 29 mass units from the molecular ion most commonly corresponds to loss of:
e: Alpha cleavage adjacent to the aldehyde carbonyl commonly ejects the formyl radical, CHO, which has a mass of 29, leaving behind a stabilized carbon-centered cation.

q: Aromatic compounds often show a strong, easily recognized molecular ion peak relative to many aliphatic compounds mainly because:
e: The aromatic ring can delocalize the positive charge and radical character of the molecular ion over the ring system, stabilizing it and making the intact M+ more likely to survive and be detected as a prominent peak.

q: In a standard mass spectrum plot, the x-axis (m/z) represents a peak's relative abundance, while the y-axis (intensity) represents its mass-to-charge ratio.
e: It is actually the reverse: the x-axis shows the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of each ion, while the y-axis shows that ion's relative intensity, or abundance, compared to the base peak.

q: When an alkane's molecular ion fragments by breaking a carbon-carbon bond, the fragmentation pathway that generates the most stable resulting carbocation (terti
e: Fragmentation in the gas phase favors pathways that produce the most stable cation, following the same substitution-based stability trend (tertiary greater than secondary greater than primary) used to rationalize carbocation stability throughout organic chemistry.

q: An unknown compound's mass spectrum shows significant fragment peaks corresponding to loss of 15 (a methyl group) and loss of 29 (an ethyl-related fragment) fro
e: Alpha cleavage on either side of an asymmetric ketone's carbonyl generates two different acylium-type cations, explaining why both a methyl loss (15) and a loss consistent with the other alkyl substituent pattern can appear together in the spectrum of a compound like methyl ethyl ketone.

q: Loss of a single hydrogen atom, a mass loss of just 1 unit, from the molecular ion is relatively uncommon as a dominant fragmentation pathway compared to loss o
e: Because forming larger, more stable radicals (or undergoing favorable rearrangements like McLafferty) is usually more thermodynamically favorable than simply ejecting a lone hydrogen atom, simple H-loss is typically a minor pathway rather than the dominant one.

q: A high-resolution mass spectrometer can distinguish between two different molecular formulas that share the same nominal (whole-number) mass, such as C2H4O and
e: Individual isotopes have exact masses that are not perfectly whole numbers (for example, carbon-12 is defined as exactly 12, but hydrogen and oxygen have slightly different fractional exact masses), so formulas with the same nominal mass usually have distinguishably different exact masses when measured with sufficient precision.

q: The relative intensity of a peak in a mass spectrum reflects the relative abundance of that particular gas-phase ion reaching the detector, which is governed by
e: Mass spectral peak intensities depend on how readily a given ion forms and survives under gas-phase ionization and fragmentation conditions, a distinct context from solution-phase stability, solubility, or reactivity, which are not what mass spectrometry intensities measure.

q: A cyclic secondary alcohol's mass spectrum can show both a loss of 18 (water) and a loss of 28 (often consistent with ethylene or CO) from the molecular ion. A
e: Molecular ions are not limited to a single fragmentation route; different bonds can break under the conditions of electron ionization, so a cyclic alcohol can plausibly show both a straightforward water loss and a separate ring-related elimination pathway in the same spectrum.

q: For a simple carboxylic acid, a loss of 45 mass units from the molecular ion typically corresponds to loss of:
e: Alpha cleavage adjacent to the carbonyl-bearing carbon of a carboxylic acid commonly ejects the COOH group, which has a combined mass of 45, leaving behind the remaining alkyl cation.

q: Why does electron ionization (EI) typically produce a radical cation (an odd-electron species) as the molecular ion, rather than an even-electron cation?
e: Since a neutral organic molecule normally has all its electrons paired, knocking out just one electron during EI necessarily leaves an odd, unpaired electron along with the resulting positive charge, producing a radical cation.

q: Combining the nitrogen rule with an observed odd molecular ion mass for a compound containing only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen, what can be concluded
e: According to the nitrogen rule, an odd molecular weight for a typical CHNO compound implies an odd number of nitrogen atoms, since each nitrogen (with its odd valence pattern) shifts the overall parity of the molecular mass.
